summary: A sequence diagram is a behavioural (interaction) diagram: objects across the top, **time flows downward**, and messages are horizontal arrows between lifelines.

The arrow style carries the meaning: **filled** head = synchronous call, **open** head = asynchronous, **dashed** line = reply/return, **dashed + `new`** into a lowered head box = creation, **X** at the bottom of a lifeline = destruction.
Found message = starts from a black dot (sender unknown). Lost message = ends at a black dot (receiver unknown).

Interaction fragments are boxes with an operator in the top-left pentagon: `opt` (if), `alt` (if-else/switch), `loop`, `break`, `par`, `critical`, `ref` (reuse another sd). Conditions are guards in `[ ]`.
Diagram to code: each arrow into an object becomes a method call on a field/local of that type; self-messages become private helper calls; `x = msg()` means the return value is assigned to `x`.
mustMemorise: Synchronous message = solid line + FILLED arrowhead (a normal method call; the caller waits).
Asynchronous message = solid line + OPEN (stick) arrowhead (the caller does not wait).
Reply/return message = DASHED line (open arrowhead), going back to the caller.
Creation = dashed line with open arrow labelled `new`, pointing at the HEAD box of the new object, drawn lower than the other heads.
Destruction = a large X at the end of the lifeline.
Found message = black dot at the START (unknown sender). Lost message = black dot at the END (never arrives).
Lifeline head format `[name] : ClassName`: the class name is mandatory, the object name is optional (e.g. `:User`, `btn:Button`).
Frame = rectangle with `sd <InteractionName>` in a pentagon at the top left.
Activation bar (execution specification) = the thin rectangle on a lifeline while a method is running.

`opt` = if (one operand). `alt` = if/else or switch (operands split by dashed lines; at most one runs). `loop` = repeat while guard. `break` = runs instead of the rest of the enclosing fragment. `par` = parallel. `critical` = no interleaving. `ref` = InteractionUse (reference to another sd).
Guard = condition in square brackets, e.g. `[isAuthenticated]`, `[else]`.

items.title: Anatomy of a sequence diagram (sd ButtonPress)
notes: `press` (User to Button) has an **open stick arrowhead** = **asynchronous**. `actionPerformed(event)` and `toggle` have **filled** heads = **synchronous** calls.
The two **dashed** arrows going right-to-left are **return messages** (Light to ButtonListener, ButtonListener to Button). Nothing returns to User: an async sender does not wait for a reply.
`getState()` loops back from Light to Light = **self message**, which opens a small nested activation bar, then returns with a short dashed arrow.
Labels: dashed vertical line = **lifeline**; thin blue rectangle = **activation** (method running); `btn:Button` = object `btn` of class Button; the big blue arrow on the left = **time goes down**.

items.title: Self vs recursive message; stereotype icons
notes: **Self message**: the arrow loops back into the **same** activation bar. **Recursive message**: the arrow loops back into a **new, nested** activation bar stacked on the first.
The green box shows what it means in code: `getState()` is called **inside** `toggle()` on the same object, i.e. `this.getState()`.
Heads here use Ch8 stereotype icons: circle with a T-bar on its left = **boundary** (`:Button`, `:Light`); circle with an arrowhead on top = **control** (`:ButtonListener`).

items.title: Creating and destroying participants
notes: **Creation**: `new` is a **dashed line with an open arrowhead** that points at the **head box** of `:UserInfo`. The head is drawn **lower** than the others because the object only exists from that moment.
`validate` and `update` are **filled** heads = synchronous calls on the new object.
**Destruction**: the **X** ends UserInfo's lifeline, so the object no longer exists. (Java has no explicit delete; the object simply becomes garbage-collectable.)
Here `submit` from the User is **filled** (synchronous), so the User has an activation bar and receives the final dashed return. Contrast slide 4, where `press` is async.

items.title: Message specification syntax
notes: `result=dispatch(today)`: argument `today` goes into parameter `dateDispatched` (an `in` parameter), and the **return value is assigned to `result`**.
`verifyTransactions(myRecords=records)`: per this slide, the caller's local `myRecords` receives the value of the **inout** parameter `records`.
Parameter directions in the class box: `in`, `out`, `inout`, e.g. `dispatch(in dateDispatched: Date): Boolean`.
**Trap:** slide 21 reads `mymsg(myint=16)` the other way round (parameter `myint` gets 16). Know both readings: `x=` **before** the message name = the return value is assigned to x.

items.title: Fragments: ref and opt with a guard
notes: `ref EstablishAccess("Illegal PIN")` = **InteractionUse**: "insert another sequence diagram here" (reuse, like calling a sub-routine).
`opt [isAuthenticated]` = **if** with no else: the contents run only when the guard is true.
`[ ... ]` in square brackets = **guard**. A `ref OpenDoor` sits nested inside the opt.
`CardOut` and `Msg("Please Enter")` go **right to left** (Access Control to User). Arrows can point either way; the head shows the receiver.

items.title: loop, alt, break and the found message
notes: `printCurrentRecords(f)` starts at a **black dot** = **found message** (the sender is outside the diagram's scope).
`loop [not end of file]` = while loop. Inside it, `alt [rec==valid] ... [else]` = **if/else** (or switch). The **dashed line** separates the operands, and at most one operand runs.
`[else] log(rec)` is a self message on PrintManager. `rec=readRecord()` means the return value is assigned to `rec`, even though no dashed reply is drawn.
Red inset: `break [y>0]` inside a loop runs `save()` and then **leaves the enclosing fragment** (the loop), like Java `break`.

items.title: Enacting a use case flow (fingerprint access)
notes: Typical layering: **Actor, then Boundary** (`:FingerprintReaderInterface`), **then Control** (`:FASMgr`, `:FingerprintMgr`), **then Entity** (`:Fingerprint`). The actor talks only to the boundary.
`result=validate(img)` is a synchronous call whose return value is assigned to `result`. Inside it, `loop [not last record and not found]` repeats `findMatch(img)`.
Dashed arrows = returns (FingerprintMgr to FASMgr; FASMgr to the reader interface).
`opt [result==true]`, then `unlock()` goes to `:EntryGateInterface` (a boundary to a device). This is how a use-case flow becomes messages.

items.title: sd CalculatePrice (the source of the code on slides 14-16)
notes: `calculatePrice()` enters from a **filled dot** = **found message**.
Calls on other objects (getQuantity, getProduct, getPricingDetails, getDiscountInfo) map to calls through **fields/locals** of Order: `ol`, `p`, `c`.
Self messages (calculateBasicPrice, calculateDiscounts, calculateTotalPrice) each open a nested activation bar and map to **private helper methods** of Order.
Dashed returns carry values: `p`, `price`, `total`. `qty = getQuantity()` shows the return by assignment instead of an arrow.

items.title: Order code: does NOT compile as written
notes: `private Orderline ol;` but the class is `OrderLine`. Java is case-sensitive, so this is **cannot find symbol**.
`p.getPricingDetail()` but Product declares `getPricingDetails()`, so this is also **cannot find symbol**.
`calculateBasicPrice(qty, price)` has **no parameter types**, so it is a syntax error. Should be `(int qty, double price)`. Checked with javac 17.

Exam: if asked for the mapping, the answer is self message = private method and arrow to another object = call through a field/local. With these typos fixed, `calculatePrice()` returns `100.0 * 10.0 = 1000.0` (`bPrice` is computed but never used, as in the diagram).

items.title: OrderLine code: syntax error
notes: `public int getQuantity( ) () {` has an **extra `()`**, which javac rejects (`';' expected`).
`calculateTotalPrice(double price, double discount)` returns `price * discount`, which matches the diagram's arguments (price, not bPrice). It is logically odd but faithful to the diagram.
Getters `getQuantity()` and `getProduct()` correspond to the synchronous arrows into `ol:OrderLine`.

items.title: Product & Customer; 'must be COMPILABLE'
notes: `getPricingDetails()` returns `100.0`. `getDiscountInfo()` returns `10.0`. Both print as doubles (`100.0`, `10.0`).
The slide insists partial code **must still be COMPILABLE**, yet slides 14-15 are not (see the notes there). In a code-writing question, give types for every parameter and match names exactly.

items.title: Frame and Lifeline definitions
notes: **Frame**: a rectangle with `sd` + the interaction name (and parameters) in a **pentagon** at the top left.
**Lifeline** = one participant: a head rectangle plus a vertical (may be dashed) line for its lifetime.
Head text format is `[name] : <class_name>`. The **class name is mandatory and the name is optional**.

items.title: Execution specification and InteractionUse
notes: **Execution Specification = Activation** (the thin bar), bounded by its start and finish occurrence specifications.
**InteractionUse** = a combined-fragment-style box with operator **`ref`**, used to share a common portion between several interactions.

items.title: Combined fragment operators
notes: `alt` = choice; **at most one** operand runs, the one whose guard is true.
`opt` = a single conditional trace; **equivalent to an `alt` with only one trace**.
`loop` = at least `minint`, at most `maxint` iterations, then stops when the guard is false. `break` = runs **instead of the remainder** of the enclosing fragment.
`par` = operands run in **parallel**. `critical` = a region that **cannot be interleaved**.

items.title: Message arrow types and destruction
notes: **Asynchronous = open arrowhead. Synchronous (operation call) = filled arrowhead.** Reply = **dashed line**. Creation = **dashed line with open arrow**.
**Destruction event = X**.
Syntax: `mymessage(14, - , 3.14, "hello")`, where `-` = undefined argument. `v=mymsg(16, variab):96` is a **reply** carrying return value 96, which is assigned to `v`.
Trap: a creation arrow and a reply arrow are both dashed. Creation is labelled `new` and points at a head box. A reply points back to the caller's activation.

items.title: Lost vs Found messages
notes: **Lost**: the sender is known but there is **no receiver**. The black dot is at the **arrow end**, e.g. a Web Client's `search` that never arrives.
**Found**: the receiver is known but the **sender is unknown or out of scope**. The black dot is at the **start**, e.g. Online Bookshop receives `search`.
Memory aid: the dot sits where the unknown end is.
